story.title: Two shared rings: how io_uring batches reads, and what it costs

tldr: io_uring gives Linux two shared rings: the app fills a submission queue, the kernel fills a completion queue, and one io_uring_enter can submit and reap many I/Os. The win is batching and concurrency, not a faster epoll: a naive swap gains only 1.06–1.10×. The price is a second syscall surface that seccomp cannot inspect.
why: Why it matters: it is now an opt-in I/O path in PostgreSQL 18, a read path in RocksDB, and the file path in several runtimes, and it is why security teams ask whether to allow it in containers at all.

cards.title: Two trays and one bell, not a walk per errand
cards.brief: A cook drops several order notes on a tray, rings one bell and keeps cooking. The helper does the quick ones at once, parks the slow ones and posts each result with its number. Many errands in flight from one thread.

cards.title: Six ideas to know first
cards.brief:
• Syscall: a user-to-kernel switch; mitigations make entry costly.
  • Readiness vs completion: epoll says "can read", completion says "the read is done".
  • Page cache vs O_DIRECT: only O_DIRECT was truly async in Linux aio.
  • SPSC ring with acquire/release on the tail.
  • Little's law: in flight = throughput × latency.

cards.title: Databases adopt it for storage; sockets are the harder half
cards.brief: PostgreSQL 18 offers io_method=io_uring (default is worker). RocksDB uses it on read paths, TigerBeetle routes all I/O through it, libuv moved file ops to it. Google disabled it on ChromeOS and production.

cards.title: “Async I/O through shared rings” hides five things
cards.brief: Most ops finish inline, not async. "No syscalls" needs SQPOLL, which burns a core. A naive swap gains only 1.06–1.10×; the redesign adds 2.05–2.31×. It is a second syscall surface that seccomp cannot see.

cards.title: Linux aio copies 104 bytes and needs two syscalls per I/O
cards.brief: Linux aio was async only for O_DIRECT, copied 104 bytes per I/O and took at least two syscalls, so apps bolted on thread pools. The paper's 4K random reads: 608K IOPS for aio, 1.2M for io_uring without polling, 1.7M with it.

cards.title: A restaurant order window: one bell for a stack of orders
cards.brief: Kitchen and diner share two belts: orders in (SQ), plates out (CQ). The diner stacks 32 slips and rings once. The cook does quick orders on the spot and parks slow ones. The analogy breaks where belts carry indexes and buffers stay yours.

cards.title: One read from SQE to CQE, usually with no thread
cards.brief:
One io_uring_enter submits the batch and the kernel tries the read inline. A socket with no data sleeps on a poll list; a buffered file falls back to an iou-wrk worker. Results come back as CQEs read from shared memory.

Seven-step walkthrough inside.

cards.title: Batching divides the syscall cost; queue depth sets IOPS
cards.brief:
Cost per op is cs/B + co, so batching only hides the entry cost. Little's law gives IOPS = QD / latency: 100 µs reads need QD ≈ 100 for 1M IOPS. Sync POSIX ran 16.5K tx/s against 376K with io_uring, mostly from queue depth.

Two sliders inside.

cards.title: Remove any one piece and it falls back to aio or a thread pool
cards.brief: The core move is turning the syscall into data. Shared rings replace copies; inline-first avoids thread handoffs; the poll path avoids a thread per socket; io-wq catches the rest. Without user_data out-of-order completions cannot be matched.

cards.title: Batch size, SQPOLL and polling trade cores for latency
cards.brief: You choose SQ depth, batch size, and whether to burn a core on SQPOLL or IOPOLL. Alternatives: epoll with threads (about 10% behind at 1,000 connections, one vendor benchmark), libaio for O_DIRECT, SPDK at about 2× the cores.

cards.title: A second syscall surface that seccomp cannot see
cards.brief: Google's kCTF: 60% of 42 Linux kernel exploit submissions targeted io_uring, so it was disabled on ChromeOS and production and blocked for Android apps. Seccomp sees only setup and enter calls, not the SQE opcodes.

cards.title: Engines use it where the win is, and deviate from the paper
cards.brief: RocksDB uses it only on read paths. libuv moved file ops to it, then reverted the default to the thread pool in v1.49. Jasny et al. report +14% for PostgreSQL after applying their guidelines. Glommio runs thread-per-core on io_uring.

cards.title: The frontier moves to zero-copy receive and BPF-run rings
cards.brief: Zero-copy receive, merged in Linux 6.15, hands NIC buffers to user space; one core saturated 200G in the demo. A BPF struct_ops series could replace the enter loop, with merge status only secondhand. Restrictions plus a cBPF filter cannot inspect arguments.

cards.title: Sandboxing io_uring without disabling it is still unsolved
cards.brief: Filters see opcodes but not safe arguments, and pointers live in shared memory (TOCTOU). Disk I/O cannot be cancelled, so a cancel can DMA into reused pages. Buffered file I/O stays on a thread pool until every filesystem has NOWAIT paths.

cards.title: Linux aio (2002) failed on copies; io_uring shipped in 5.1 (2019)
cards.brief: Linux aio was O_DIRECT-only and copy-heavy, while Windows IOCP was completion-based from the 1990s. io_uring then gained fixed resources and multishot (5.19), DEFER_TASKRUN (6.0–6.1), NVMe passthrough, zero-copy receive (6.15) and BPF rings targeted for 7.1.

cards.title: A 30-line program shows the syscall count and the inline/punt split
cards.brief: Read 64 blocks per round, count io_uring_enter calls with strace, then drop caches to watch iou-wrk threads appear. Predict first. Needs Linux 5.19+ and liburing. The author did not compile it; run it on your kernel.

cards.title: Test yourself
cards.brief: 24 questions from mechanism to open research. Reveal, then mark ✓ or ✗; marks feed your progress ring.

cards.title: Three dives that build on this
cards.brief: NVMe queue pairs and SPDK polling; TCP zero-copy with page_pool and flow steering; kernel object lifetimes and the LPE work behind the io_uring CVE stream.

cards.title: Each number traces to a paper, kernel doc or primary post
cards.brief: Axboe 2019, Jasny et al. VLDB'26, Pestka et al., Joshi et al. FAST'24, kernel and liburing docs, Google's kCTF post and the CVE write-ups. Tags: [V] checked against a source; [K] unverified.

cold.q: What did a naive libaio-to-io_uring swap gain in a database buffer manager?
cold.reveal: 1.06×. A drop-in swap barely moves the buffer manager. Jasny et al. (PVLDB 2026) get 2.05× only after redesigning it around completions and batching.

problem.q: On 4K random reads with no polling, how much faster was io_uring than Linux aio?
problem.reveal: About 2×. The paper measured 1.2M IOPS for io_uring without polling and 608K for aio. With polling it reached 1.7M.

math.q: Sync POSIX ran 16.5K transactions per second in one buffer-manager thread. How much did io_uring reach?
math.reveal: About 376K, roughly 23× more. Little's law says most of that gap is queue depth: many requests in flight from one thread, not only the saved syscalls.

knobs.q: At 1,000 connections, how far ahead of tuned epoll did io_uring run in one vendor benchmark?
knobs.reveal: About 10%. Alibaba Cloud's comparison, with CPU mitigations on, reports io_uring about 10% higher than epoll. It is one vendor benchmark, and no raw numbers were published.

breaks.q: Google's kCTF study of 42 Linux kernel exploit submissions: what share targeted io_uring?
breaks.reveal: 60%. The Google Security Blog kCTF post (June 2023) reports that 60% of the submissions exploited io_uring. Google then disabled it on ChromeOS and production servers.

questions.q: What exactly happens, step by step, from io_uring_submit() for a socket read with no data yet?
questions.a: SQE written, tail released; enter → io_submit_sqes → io_queue_sqe → inline io_issue_sqe with NONBLOCK → socket returns -EAGAIN → io_queue_async copies SQE → io_arm_poll_handler → APOLL_OK: request sleeps on socket waitqueue (no thread). Data arrives → wakeup → io_poll_task_func (task_work) rechecks with vfs_poll, reissues, posts CQE.

questions.q: Why does the SQ ring hold indexes into array[] rather than SQEs, and what did 6.6 change?
questions.a: Lets apps submit non-contiguous SQEs / embed SQEs in own structs. NO_SQARRAY (6.6) removes the extra load and the indirection when apps don't need it.

questions.q: How does the kernel know the app has freed an SQE slot, and why is that safe with in-flight requests?
questions.a: Kernel smp_store_release(sq.head) after consuming (io_commit_sqring); app acquires head. Safe because the kernel copies the SQE into the request (io_req_sqe_copy, FEAT_SUBMIT_STABLE 5.5) when it will need it later; user buffers aren't copied — you must keep those alive.

questions.q: What does CQE_F_MORE mean for multishot recv and SEND_ZC, and how do the two differ?
questions.a: MORE on multishot: request still armed, more CQEs will come; absence ⇒ re-arm. MORE on SEND_ZC: a second F_NOTIF CQE follows meaning "buffer reusable"; the first CQE carries bytes sent.

questions.q: Why must SQPOLL's NEED_WAKEUP flow have a full barrier on both sides?
questions.a: Store-load ordering (Dekker): app stores tail then loads flag; thread stores flag then loads tail. Without a full barrier both can read stale values → app sees no flag, thread sees no entries → sleeps forever with work pending.

questions.q: What is task_work, and why does DEFER_TASKRUN require SINGLE_ISSUER?
questions.a: task_work = a callback run in the context of a specific task at kernel→user transition (or an explicit point). DEFER_TASKRUN runs it only within io_uring_enter(GETEVENTS) on the ring's work_llist; only the submitter task may reap, hence single issuer.

questions.q: Why try inline non-blocking first rather than always queue?
questions.a: Most ops (page-cache hit, ready socket, NOWAIT O_DIRECT) finish immediately; queueing costs ≥2 context switches. Inline = no handoff, CQE ready on return.

questions.q: Why two io-wq pools (bound/unbound)?
questions.a: Bound ops (regular files/bdev) have bounded concurrency tied to the device queue; unbound (sockets) can block indefinitely; mixing would let slow sockets starve disk work or force an arbitrary cap.

questions.q: Why are free-running indexes better than wrapping indexes?
questions.a: Full vs empty distinguishable without a wasted slot; all N usable; modular subtraction handles u32 wrap.

questions.q: Why do provided buffer rings make multishot recv scale better than epoll+read for idle connections?
questions.a: Provided buffers are picked at data arrival, so idle connections hold no buffer; epoll+read typically needs a buffer per connection (or read-after-ready, which still needs a buffer at that time but costs a syscall each).

questions.q: If CQ were exactly SQ size and no NODROP, what breaks?
questions.a: A burst of completions exceeds CQ while the app is busy ⇒ completions dropped (pre-5.5) or must be stored; with NODROP they pile in kernel memory until the app enters; extreme case: lost/stalled completions.

questions.q: If io-wq workers were kernel threads (pre-5.12) not process threads, what changes for cgroups/creds/ptrace?
questions.a: Kernel threads: separate creds/cgroup/ptrace invisibility, harder accounting, no RLIMIT_NPROC coupling; 5.12 made them process threads: inherit cgroup/creds, visible to ptrace/coredump (and regressions).

questions.q: If SEND_ZC had no notification CQE, what could go wrong?
questions.a: App reuses/frees the buffer while the NIC still DMAs from it ⇒ corrupted data on the wire or use-after-free of page contents.

questions.q: If the kernel read your SQE lazily (after returning) without copying it, what bug appears?
questions.a: App reuses the slot, kernel executes the new SQE (or a half-written one) ⇒ wrong op/args. Hence copy-on-defer.

questions.q: How would you hide file exfiltration from a seccomp+Falco setup using io_uring?
questions.a: Do exfil via SQEs: OPENAT, READ, SEND/CONNECT ops; seccomp sees only enter; Falco hooks syscalls → blind (ARMO Curing).

questions.q: Where is the TOCTOU surface when the kernel reads shared-memory SQEs?
questions.a: Kernel reads SQE fields from user-writable memory (after READ_ONCE); an app thread can mutate the SQE or pointed-to structs concurrently. A per-opcode filter that inspects args at filter time may see different values than at execution; the kernel mitigates by copying the SQE before use, but pointer targets (iovecs, msghdr) remain user memory.

questions.q: How could a registered-buffer bug give physical-memory access (cf. CVE-2023-2598)?
questions.a: Fixed-buffer registration coalesces pages into compound-page folios; wrong arithmetic computes a buffer range/length past the folio ⇒ read/write to adjacent physical pages through the registered buffer ⇒ kernel memory R/W ⇒ LPE.

questions.q: How would you DoS a host using only unprivileged io_uring and RLIMIT_NPROC?
questions.a: Queue many blocking unbound ops (e.g., reads on a socket/pipe that never gets data) across many ring-submitting threads: each can spawn io-wq workers up to RLIMIT_NPROC (per-user), starving the user/container of threads; with pids.max, workers burn CPU retrying creation.

questions.q: Compare io_uring's SQ/CQ with NVMe's submission/completion queues. What does passthrough remove?
questions.a: Same producer/consumer queue pair idea; io_uring has an extra software layer (block layer, page cache, FS). Passthrough (URING_CMD + /dev/ng*) skips block layer/FS so the NVMe SQE goes nearly straight to the device queue; you give up caching, FS semantics, LBA mgmt (16–40% IOPS gain in FAST'24).

questions.q: How does completion-based I/O change Rust's Future cancellation model?
questions.a: Rust futures are cancelled by drop; with readiness that's safe. With completion, the kernel may still write into your buffer after drop ⇒ UB. Fix: ownership transfer of buffers (tokio-uring style APIs) or cancel-and-wait; cost: ergonomics, no &mut [u8] APIs.

questions.q: How is Little's law behind both NVMe queue depth and why sync I/O is slow?
questions.a: IOPS = QD/latency: the device has ~µs–100 µs latency, so to reach 1M IOPS you need ~100 in flight. Sync I/O has QD=1/thread; io_uring/NVMe queues allow deep QD from one thread.

questions.q: Can a sandbox filter io_uring per-op without TOCTOU and without disabling it?
questions.a: Open. Needs filtering at the semantic level (opcode + stable args) with a TOCTOU-safe copy; the current cBPF filter doesn't inspect args. Alternative: capability-style per-ring restrictions (existing REGISTER_RESTRICTIONS) — coarse.

questions.q: Can buffered file I/O ever be truly async on Linux without per-filesystem NOWAIT work?
questions.a: Open. Requires NOWAIT support for allocation, journalling, writeback throttling in each FS; or accept the thread pool as the implementation (what io-wq is).

questions.q: Should the ring be BPF-programmable, or does that grow the attack surface faster than it removes syscalls?
questions.a: Open. BPF removes syscalls and enables custom completion logic but adds a verified-code attack surface and interaction with cancellation; the history of BPF verifier bugs argues caution; the unprivileged cBPF filter is the conservative variant.
